newsitem.title: KYRGYZSTAN: FEATURE - For Kyrgyz drug addicts, home is no place for cure.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - For Kyrgyz drug addicts, home is no place for cure.

text.p: Gulya sat hunched forward in the tiny kitchen watching and waiting as her friend worked on her favourite recipe.
The 23-year-old former schoolteacher wasn't hungry but craving for her thrice-daily opium fix.
"My appetite only comes back after injecting," she said.
Dilshat, 21, prepared the opium with all the care and finesse of a master chef, but his slurred voice and empty staring eyes showed he was on the same deadly diet as Gulya.
The two are among a growing army of drug addicts in this former Soviet republic in Central Asia, where opium from Afghanistan is easily obtained.
The people here are poor, with an average salary of about $50 a month, but some sell everything they own, borrow or steal to pay for their expensive habit.
For the drug traders, it is still more profitable to send their lethal cargoes north to Kazakhstan, Russia and Europe.

Opium prices rise sharply along the smuggling chain, from about $100 per kg (2.2 lb) in Afghanistan to $400 in the lawless Gorno-Badakshan region of Tajikistan and $1,000 in Osh, a drug-trafficking centre in western Kyrgyzstan.
The same quantity might fetch $10,000 in Russia and much more in Western Europe.
In Osh, one of the oldest Central Asian cities, and in the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek, there are some streets where you can buy opium in every house.
Market reforms have left many people in the republic of 4.4 million disoriented, if not impoverished, and the government lacks resources to mount an effective campaign against drug abuse.
Gulya, who has a six-year-old daughter, was aware of the dangers and said she had tried to kick the habit.

"I wouldn't wish this on anyone. We'd like to find a way out," she said. "But there's always a voice in your mind that keeps telling you "I want it. I want it.' Then you say "Just once more. Then I'll give it up.'"
Gulya's story of a life in ruins, jobless and a husband in prison, is typical of many addicts in Osh, a market town less than 750 km (466 miles) from the Afghan border.

The drug problem is fairly new to Kyrgyzstan. Before the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, the very existence of addiction was officially denied and, like prostitution, it was considered an evil exclusive to the capitalist world.
But the dismantling of tight Soviet police controls allowed the once-hidden drug culture to develop into a crisis that current authorities are struggling to handle.
"We had no means of tackling the problem," said Timur Issakov, deputy head of the Kyrgyz Interior Ministry's anti-drug department.
In a raid on a flat in Osh, near the border with Uzbekistan, Farid, a drug squad officer, said: "All the women here are injecting."
One of the women was hysterical and clutching a baby in her pock-marked arms as police with a spaniel sniffer dog searched for and found drugs in syringes, ready for use.
Khamat, 29, said her brother had died from an overdose and her husband was in prison. "I want to stop it. I didn't know what the consequences would be."

Another woman, Saida, 35, had given up and believed anyone with the willpower to do so could succeed. "I was injecting for five years and gave up in March. I had to. I was caught by the police," she said.
"But it hurts everywhere, your kidneys, heart, liver."
As Dilshat prepared Gulya's dose in another part of the city, he explained how difficult it is to resist temptation during "cold turkey", the painful withdrawal process.
"If you give it up, you'll still run into old friends. To give up you have to go somewhere where they are not." Other addicts said the same -- there's no place worse than home.
As he spoke, Dilshat removed the brown opium gum from the small polythene packets in which single doses are sold. "I saw how this was done and gradually learned to do it myself," he said.
He scraped the opium with a knife into a soup ladle, added pure vinegar and heated the mixture over the gas cooker, taking extreme pains not to lose a drop.

Then he purified the liquid, drawing it through a syringe with a clean cigarette butt on the end of the needle. Any chocolate, flour or other substances mixed in with the opium were left in the ladle.
The opium was heated again in a pot until it dried out. Dilshat, wiping sweat from his brow, cooled the pot by running the outside of it under cold water.

After adding a few more ingredients for an extra kick and some water, he stirred the brown liquid and the recipe was complete. The whole process took about 25 minutes before Dilshat shot it into Gulya's forearm. "Immediate, complete relaxation," was how she described the sensation.
